overview.title: Reading Jewish Łódź through its memorial book
overview.summary: Before the Holocaust, Łódź was home to a large, diverse Jewish community deeply involved in industry, commerce, medicine, education, religion, politics, and culture. The memorial book follows that community from ordinary family and institutional life through German occupation, ghetto confinement, forced labor, deportation, murder, resistance, and survival. It also shows how survivors rebuilt lives, organized communal institutions, and created commemorative records after the destruction. By following the paths below, readers can understand both the scale of the loss and the human relationships, choices, and cultural life that made Jewish Łódź a community.

paths.title: What kind of Jewish city was Łódź before the war?
paths.description: This path introduces Łódź as a major Jewish urban community shaped by work, migration, neighborhood life, and relationships with other populations. By the end, readers will see the city as a lived society rather than only the later site of a ghetto.
paths.question: How did Jewish life take shape in Łódź?

steps.title: A large and diverse community
steps.summary: The memorial book describes a Jewish community of nearly a quarter of a million people before 1939. It places Jews within a city also inhabited by Poles and Germans, with Jews and Germans together making up nearly 40 percent of the population in one account. [mention_359e7216d59a25e03734a45f, mention_f2a62067810201dbf446b7e5, mention_52c4993a757aa955cfb73afd]

steps.summary: Jewish life was connected to Łódź’s industrial economy: Israel Poznanski is remembered as a major manufacturer who built housing for workers’ families and supported Jewish charities. steps.summary: Personal recollections place family life in homes, streets, shops, schools, and cafés: one narrator arrived at the Łódź railway station to join many relatives, while another recalls a family home and a food business on Wschodnia Street. paths.title: How did Łódź Jews educate, worship, create, and organize?
paths.description: This path traces the institutions and debates that sustained Jewish identity across religious, educational, political, literary, theatrical, and sporting life. Readers will understand the community as internally varied, energetic, and culturally productive.
paths.question: What ideas and institutions shaped Jewish Łódź?

steps.title: Schools and learning
steps.summary: Jewish education ranged from a yeshiva and gymnasium education to vocational and girls’ secondary schools. The book names institutions such as the Jaroczynski Vocational School, the Second Gymnasium, Wolfson School, and Beit Ulpana Gymnasium, established by the Mizrahi organization. [mention_3fd8be7cd6753efdc55b897f, mention_9a13fd5c5498fc4f80684cd6, mention_118aa98f6e08c4c0cb2eb592, mention_e65e9b19d7a260823689df37, mention_9638120228af1a5275ed0ec4]

steps.summary: Religious life included Hasidic dynasties and synagogues, including the Radoshitzer tradition and Poznanski’s synagogue. The memorial book also remembers an official ghetto synagogue where Moshe Tafel served as cantor, linking prewar religious structures to wartime experience. steps.title: Politics and associations
steps.summary: Łódź Jews participated in competing political movements, including the Bund, Poale Zion, the Folkists, General Zionists, and Gordonia. These movements also shaped unions, libraries, youth activity, and elections, revealing disagreement alongside organized communal participation. steps.title: Literature, theater, music, and sport
steps.summary: The book describes Łódź as a literary center with Yiddish and Hebrew writers, newspapers, libraries, theaters, and a first Hebrew theater troupe. Cultural life also included the Hakoah sports club and a Jewish Theater Studio, showing how language, performance, reading, and recreation connected people across the city. paths.title: How did occupation transform everyday life?
paths.description: This path follows the transition from invasion to confinement, hunger, forced labor, administrative control, and cultural survival. Readers will learn how the ghetto was both a system of persecution and a place where people continued to work, teach, create, and care for one another.
paths.question: How did German rule reshape Łódź Jewish life?

steps.title: Invasion and the tearing apart of families
steps.summary: The memorial book recalls Hitler’s army entering Łódź and young Jewish men fleeing toward Russia. It describes Jewish family life as rapidly torn apart by persecution, establishing the violent rupture between prewar life and occupation. [event_candidate_47edb3593260c946d0ba7b0f, mention_ea3c53dc97a60fa0714ccdeb]

steps.title: Confinement and imposed administration
steps.summary: By April 1940, Moshe Tafel had entered the Łódź ghetto, where access and communication were controlled and Jewish police were described as serving German power. The ghetto’s administration, including Rumkowski and the Jewish Order Service, became part of a coercive system that governed residents’ lives. [event_candidate_8ed6f5a3b491d2233705d959, mention_8e435081c21e60a50e8876c9, mention_e5bc6c228626d9a4dcc58c8e, mention_094aebbfd408c408ac700bb4]

steps.summary: Thousands of young people registered for work outside the ghetto, while workshops expanded into varied trades and began taking orders from the outside world. steps.title: Hunger, children, and deportation
steps.summary: The book identifies May through September 1942 as the ghetto’s hardest period because of severe hunger, while children and older people faced registration, searches, and removal. steps.summary: Even under ghetto conditions, libraries, music, theater, and youth activities continued. paths.title: How did destruction unfold, and how did people resist?
paths.description: This path moves from deportation transports and mass murder to individual acts of defiance, hiding, and rescue. It presents the memorial book’s testimony as a record of both organized destruction and people’s attempts to protect life and dignity.
paths.question: What happened to the ghetto’s people, and what forms of resistance were possible?

steps.title: The transports began
steps.summary: The book records a first transport to Chełmno from Radegast station on 16 January 1942 and a final transport numbered 80 on 2 April 1942. A letter remembered by Rabbi Silman reported that people were being killed at Chełmno, giving the transports a deadly meaning within the testimony. [event_candidate_ef9a382830d1e81483ff3cfe, event_candidate_3c108d9977067d6bac81e9aa, mention_2c34ecfa7c45761d21a7d3a5, event_candidate_bdb59e94ebd2aff16241d566]

steps.summary: Resistance included demonstrations against Rumkowski’s administration, a September 1940 tailors’ strike, and children’s collective protest over a withheld lunch. steps.title: Hiding and rescue
steps.summary: Jakub Pazuanski, his wife, and daughter hid for ten weeks at Papir Resort, while Dr. Weisskopf hid in a bunker and attacked ghetto commandant Hans Bibow with his bare hands. The book also recalls efforts to save orphan children from deportation to the Chełmno gas chambers. paths.title: What did survival and rebuilding look like after the destruction?
paths.description: This path follows liberation, displacement, migration, communal reconstruction, and the preservation of testimony. Readers will see that survival was not a single ending but a long process involving illness, family loss, new homes, institutions, and public memory.
paths.question: How did survivors rebuild lives and remember Łódź?

steps.title: Liberation amid loss
steps.summary: The memorial book describes people being liberated individually in the Łódź ghetto and another narrator being saved after a Russian advance guard caused German forces to flee. Other testimony records parents dying of hunger, showing that liberation came amid profound physical and family loss. [event_candidate_cde5c376c6951e98c772283d, event_candidate_908e3fbd9a4d0c0a9699f388, event_candidate_acf67891bc8bc4eceee4a30f]

steps.title: Displacement and new lives
steps.summary: Survivors moved through camps and countries: one account reaches liberation on 18 April 1948, while H. Rozhaner settled in Melbourne in 1952 and continued practicing medicine. These accounts show survival as both recovery from persecution and the creation of lives far from Łódź. steps.title: Public remembrance
steps.summary: The book recalls that the liquidation of the Łódź ghetto was not publicly commemorated by Łódź Jews in one period, while an annual Warsaw Ghetto Uprising commemoration served to express mourning for Łódź Jewry. A monument to the martyrs of Łódź was finally unveiled on 27 September 1989, making remembrance a visible public act.
